html:
How this works

TX-NOMINATE places every member of the Texas House and Senate on a map using nothing but their record votes. Members who vote alike end up close together, and members who usually vote against each other end up far apart. It's a Texas version of DW-NOMINATE, the method behind Voteview's maps of Congress.

60,954record votes, 74th–89th Legislatures (1995–2025)
30,627contested votes used to draw the map
617legislators placed
2,394,253individual yea and nay votes

Reading the map

  • Left to right: liberal to conservative. The main divide in Texas votes. Today it's almost entirely Democrats against Republicans; in the 1990s, when many rural and South Texas Democrats voted conservatively, the parties overlapped much more.
  • Up and down: establishment to anti-establishment. The second divide separates members who vote with their chamber's leadership from those who buck it, within both parties. Among House Republicans the top is each era's Speaker's team: Talmadge Heflin and Fred Hill under Craddick, Four Price and Stan Lambert more recently. The bottom is the rebels: the anti-Craddick Republicans of 2007–09 (Tommy Merritt, Delwin Jones), then Jonathan Stickland, Brian Harrison and Andy Hopper. Among Democrats, mavericks like Terry Canales sit lowest. In the Senate the axis separates institutionalists such as Robert Nichols and Charles Schwertner from members such as Mayes Middleton and Sarah Eckhardt.
  • Scores run from −1 to +1 and only describe positions relative to other Texas legislators. A "moderate" here is someone between the parties' blocs in Austin, not a moderate by any national standard.
  • Only contested votes count. A vote counts as contested when at least 2.5% of those voting were on the losing side. Most record votes are near-unanimous and say nothing about who disagrees with whom. They're still listed in the vote explorer.
  • On a vote's page, the dashed line is the cutting line. It's where the model draws the split for that vote: members on the shaded side are expected to vote yea, members on the other side nay. Members on the "wrong" side are the surprises.

How many dimensions?

The model can use as many axes as you like, but each additional one has to earn its place. Here's how well the map predicts members' yea and nay votes with one, two and three dimensions:

DimensionsVotes predicted correctlyAPRE
190.4%0.59
291.4%0.63
392.0%0.65

APRE (aggregate proportional reduction in error) is the share of the losing-side votes the model gets right beyond the trivial guess that everyone voted with the majority. 0 means no better than that guess and 1 means perfect.

The second dimension earns its place: it cuts the remaining errors noticeably. A third adds about two-thirds as much again, because Texas votes are less one-dimensional than Congress's. But it doesn't have a clear, stable meaning yet, so the maps show the first two. We'll revisit that as older legislatures are added.

Where the votes come from

  • The official House and Senate Journals, which list how each member voted on every record vote. They come from the Legislature's journal site (House from 1995, Senate from 1999) and, for the 1995–97 Senate, the Legislative Reference Library's copies.
  • Who's who comes from the Library's Texas Legislators: Past & Present: names, parties, districts and exact service dates.
  • The journals name members by surname ("Bell, C.", "Taylor of Collin", "Mr. Speaker"). Each name is matched to one member using that session's roster, initials, counties and service dates. Where the Senate prints only the nays and absentees, the yeas are everyone else serving that day.
  • Every roll call is checked name by name against the totals printed in the journal. 272 roll calls whose names couldn't be matched exactly are left out rather than guessed.

The method

DW-NOMINATE (Poole and Rosenthal) gives each legislator an ideal point and each roll call two outcomes, yea and nay, placed in the same space. A legislator tends to vote for whichever outcome is closer, with some randomness. The positions that best explain every vote at once are the map. Each member keeps one position for their whole career, which is DW-NOMINATE's "constant" model. We tried letting positions drift in a straight line, as Voteview does for Congress. Over these 30 years that let the whole map slowly rotate, so that "left–right" meant something different in 1995 than in 2025. Holding positions fixed keeps each axis meaning the same thing in every session. The House and Senate share one scale, linked by the 32 members who served in both chambers.

We wrote our own implementation from the published model, because Voteview's code isn't licensed for reuse. To check it, we ran it on U.S. House votes from the 110th–117th Congresses (2007–2022). In one dimension our scores correlate 0.988 with Voteview's published DW-NOMINATE scores (0.90 or better within each party). Second dimensions are harder to compare. Voteview's comes from one fit of every Congress since 1789, anchored by the era of the Solid South, while a fit of 2007–2022 alone finds that era's own second divide, so the two correlate only 0.40.

Against Shor and McCarty's state legislator scores, the standard academic measure, our first dimension correlates 0.91 across 522 Texas legislators: 0.82 among Democrats and 0.68 among Republicans. Theirs combine roll calls with a national candidate survey, so they won't match exactly.

Caveats

  • Record votes aren't the whole story. Much of the Legislature's work happens in committee and in what never comes to a vote.
  • The Speaker rarely votes, so a Speaker's position comes mostly from their votes before taking the gavel.
  • Members with fewer than 20 contested votes aren't placed on the map, though their votes still appear in the explorer.
  • "Liberal" and "conservative" are labels for the axis, not verdicts on any member. The axis is simply the line along which Texas votes split most often.

Data and code

Download the data: members.csv, member_scores.csv (positions by legislature), rollcalls.csv.gz, votes.csv.gz. The code that builds everything, from downloading the journals to fitting the model, is on GitHub.

Coming next: older legislatures, back to statehood in 1846, read from the Library's scanned journals.

Built 2026-10-22. Scores are re-estimated as more history is added, so they can shift a little between versions.
